analysis.title: Claude Rates Anthropic A 2 Out Of 10: Howard Marks Asks AI What It Thinks Of AI, Days Before The $1 Trillion IPO
key_insights: Howard Marks' memo 'A Layman Thinks About AI' says the AI trade has six uncertain variables (technology, compute demand, competitive structure, beneficiaries, financing, timing). At a 60% chance on each, the odds of getting all six right are about 5%.

Marks asked Claude to score the predictability of AI subsectors on a 1-10 scale. Overall AI scored about 3. Direction of AI scored 6-7, while profits, speed and who keeps them scored about 2. Frontier labs, including Anthropic, scored 2, which Marks reads as 'practically unknowable'.

Subsector scores from Claude: regulated utilities serving AI load 6, long-term leased data centers 5-6, hyperscalers 5, chips 4 (comparable: airlines and shipping), speculative neocloud data centers 2-3 (comparable: telecom and fiber in 1998-2001), frontier labs 2 (comparable: early-stage VC).

Marks argues transformative technologies do not necessarily reward investors. If several models become equally capable, the service becomes an undifferentiated commodity sold on price and the gains go to users. The article cites the price of a given level of model performance falling roughly 13x per year.

Marks says the infrastructure route is not a layup. The data center shell is a small part of cost, chips are most of it and carry the obsolescence risk, and site acquisition, local opposition, fiber, power, cooling and financing add friction. Data center construction moratoriums succeeded last week, which could raise the value of existing capacity.

The article reports 45 data center ballot measures across the US, with one going the industry's way, and says the Nasdaq 100 had its worst day since Covid last Thursday on fears that planned capacity could be frozen by as much as 45%.

Per FactSet, Alphabet and Amazon booked $151B of gains on equity investments in Q2, mostly on Anthropic and SpaceX (which now includes xAI), making them top contributors to S&P 500 earnings. Per JPMorgan, 42 AI-related companies generated about two-thirds of S&P price gains since January 2024.

Citing Goldman, AI-related debt issuance is nearly $600B globally this year, about $400B of it in US IG, over one-fifth of total supply. AI is about 12% of the Bloomberg USD IG Corporate index and about 6% of high yield. Marks expects AI to need about $1T of new capital a year, with hundreds of billions from debt.

Marks suggests rate-insensitive hyperscaler debt demand could push up the rates the government pays. He lists credit structure risks: lease out clauses tied to 99.9% reliability, debt collateralized by chips that may not outlive the loan, off-balance-sheet SPVs, and circular financing among suppliers and customers.

Anthropic's IPO includes a $26B private placement in which every cornerstone buyer is also a supplier. Anthropic is raising roughly $100B including the placement and greenshoe, with pricing next Wednesday night and trading Thursday Nov. 19. Traditional US IPOs raised under $50B in eight of the last ten years, so one deal equals about two typical years of IPO supply.

Marks concludes that whether AI earns adequate returns on the trillions invested is 'largely a matter of faith' and that the appropriateness of stock prices and debt yields cannot be judged until it is known how AI gets used and who profits. The article's own take is that the market pays the largest premium for the least predictable segment, and that lenders face concentrated single-industry risk.

sector_views.rationale: Marks says data centers are not a layup given chip obsolescence, power, financing and local opposition. Moratoriums could favor incumbents with built, leased and powered capacity.

The article says AI-related debt is concentrated in one industry and about 12% of the Bloomberg USD IG index, and that lenders must be exceptionally vigilant. Hyperscaler debt demand may raise Treasury yields.

earnings_insights: Per FactSet, Alphabet and Amazon booked $151B of gains on equity investments in Q2, mostly marked up on Anthropic and SpaceX, making them top contributors to S&P 500 earnings. The article says this means part of index earnings is AI companies marking up stakes in other AI companies.
risk_factors: Concentration of S&P 500 earnings and price gains in AI-related companies.
AI debt concentrated in a single industry, with about $400B of US IG issuance this year and about 12% of the Bloomberg USD IG Corporate index.
Chip-collateralized debt may outlive the useful life of the chips, and some data center leases let tenants walk if reliability falls below 99.9%.
Circular financing, where money goes from A to B to financing for C, which spends it with A. Anthropic's $26B placement has only supplier cornerstone buyers.
Hyperscaler debt demand may raise government borrowing costs.
Falling price per unit of model capability (about 13x per year) and the risk that frontier models become commodities.
Possible new taxes on AI if it replaces workers and payroll tax revenue falls.
Equity and debt funding for AI may compete for the same finite IPO and capital pool.
Data center construction moratoriums and local opposition.
vol_and_positioning: The article says the Nasdaq 100 had its worst day since Covid last Thursday on data center capacity fears.
The article says the 42 AI-related companies account for about two-thirds of S&P 500 price gains since January 2024, which implies index concentration in one sector.
geopolitical: Data center moratoriums passed in ballot measures across the US last week. The article ties them to a Democratic sweep and says up to 45% of planned capacity could be frozen.
cross_bank_references: Citing Goldman, Marks writes that AI-related debt issuance has hit nearly $600 billion globally this year
per JPMorgan, a group of 42 AI-related companies has generated about two-thirds of the S&P's price gains since January 2024
Goldman's credit strategists admitted their bear case wasn't bearish enough as AI stress hit bonds

tension_points.bull_case: The technology is real and its direction is fairly predictable (Claude scores 6-7), and it will keep improving and spread through the economy.
tension_points.bear_case: Profits, timing and who keeps them score about 2. Model prices fall about 13x per year, the frontier labs are close to binary, and the market pays a premium for the least predictable segment.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Anthropic's IPO outcome on Nov. 19, which the article says will show whether the 2 out of 10 score was too harsh or too generous.

tension_points.bull_case: AI demand for capital is large and the technology is real, so borrowers have strong revenue prospects.
tension_points.bear_case: Debt is concentrated in one industry, relies on future compute revenue, and includes chip collateral, SPVs and circular deals. Lenders need to be exceptionally vigilant.
